lines.text: Hi, I'm Sindy! Today, we're putting a real Slurm cluster into your CI pipeline.
Your code talks to Slurm, but in CI, it often talks to a mock. Then the first real cluster finds what the mock never could.
All you need is a CI runner with Docker, and sind.
Say you build a workflow engine, a web portal or a client library that submits jobs to Slurm.
Every pull request should meet a real cluster. Parallel jobs must not collide, failure tests should be quick, and your scripts need output they can parse.
On GitHub, one step does it all: the sind action installs sind and creates your clusters.
You don't need special runners: the standard Ubuntu ones work, on x sixty-four and ARM, with their own Docker daemon and without sudo.
Elsewhere, all sind needs is a rootful Docker daemon. The job downloads the release binary, and checks that the sind release workflow built it.
Then it installs sind, runs sind doctor to verify the prerequisites, and creates the cluster from your config file.
If a required check fails, sind doctor exits with a non-zero status, and the job stops right there.
Now, parallel jobs. When jobs share one Docker daemon, like on a self-hosted runner, give each job its own realm.
A realm is a namespace with its own mesh network, DNS and SSH, and its own clusters. Different realms can't see each other.
Pick the realm with the realm flag, or set the sind realm variable once for the whole job.
A realm in the config file applies to create cluster alone, so pass the same realm to the commands that follow.
Why not share one realm? Its lock protects the mesh, but a single delete cluster all would wipe every job's clusters at once.
On one machine, it looks like this. Two realms each create a cluster named app, without a clash.
And you delete each one on its own, too.
Your scripts need answers they can parse, and sind speaks JSON.
sind version with the json flag prints one JSON object. The sind action reads its version field.
Like every sind get command, sind doctor takes output json, and gives each check a name, a status and a detail.
Scripts can also branch on the exit status. Zero means success, and one means the command ran and failed.
Two means sind rejected the command line, and a hundred and thirty means something interrupted it.
Here, an extra argument is a usage error, so sind exits with two. Retrying won't help, the command line has to change.
Last, failure tests. As in episode seven, a slurmd timeout of thirty marks a lost worker down within about forty seconds, not five minutes.
On a runner, nodes mount the job's workspace, so files root writes there may need sudo to clean up.
Pass data volume, and the cluster leaves the workspace alone.
A cluster config counts as much as a script with Docker access. Never build clusters from one that an untrusted pull request can edit.
A job timeout can kill sind while it holds the realm lock. The cleanup step, or any later sind command in that job, removes it.
So: a real Slurm in every run, a realm for every job, and scripts that parse JSON, check exit codes and fail fast.
Your pipeline has a real Slurm now! Next up: bring your own provisioning. See you there!
